event: Fall of Edessa to Zengi — the first Crusader state falls. The County of Edessa is destroyed. Shockwaves reach Europe and trigger the Second Crusade.
The Second Crusade fails at Damascus. The crusaders besiege the city for four days, then retreat in humiliation. Muslim confidence grows.
Battle of Hattin — Saladin destroys the Crusader field army near the Sea of Galilee. Jerusalem falls within three months. The Crusader States are reduced to a coastal strip.
The Third Crusade begins. Richard the Lionheart of England, Philip II of France, and Frederick Barbarossa of Germany march east to reclaim Jerusalem.
Siege of Acre — Richard the Lionheart takes the city after a brutal two-year siege. Acre becomes the new Crusader capital, replacing fallen Jerusalem.
Treaty of Jaffa — Richard and Saladin agree a three-year truce. Christians may visit Jerusalem as pilgrims but cannot hold or fortify it.
The Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople instead of liberating Jerusalem. Venetian manipulation diverts the crusade. Christendom is scandalized.
Treaty of Jaffa — Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II negotiates Jerusalem's return through diplomacy with Sultan al-Kamil. No blood is shed. The pope is furious.
Khwarezmian mercenaries storm Jerusalem and sack the city. Jerusalem falls for the last time. It will not be under Christian control again.
Battle of Mansurah and capture of King Louis IX. The Seventh Crusade collapses in the Nile Delta. France pays an enormous ransom.
Venetian and Genoese merchants compete fiercely for control of Acre's harbor. Trade in spices, silk, and sugar flows west to Europe at enormous profit.
Acre is the richest port in the eastern Mediterranean. Merchants from Pisa, Genoa, and Venice maintain separate walled quarters within the city.
Sugar production in the Crusader States reaches its peak. Crusader lords grow wealthy from the cane fields around Tyre and the Jordan Valley.
Saladin permits Christian pilgrims to visit the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem after the conquest. The city is Muslim-held but pilgrimage continues.
The Fourth Lateran Council calls for a new crusade. Pope Innocent III demands that Christian rulers stop fighting each other and focus on the Holy Land.
Francis of Assisi crosses enemy lines during the Fifth Crusade to preach to Sultan al-Kamil. The sultan listens politely and sends him home unharmed.
Food is desperately scarce in Acre during the siege. Soldiers boil leather for broth. A loaf of bread costs a gold piece. Horses are slaughtered for meat.
Dysentery and fever sweep through the crusader camps outside Acre. More men die of disease than of Saracen swords. The water is foul.
The Italian merchant quarters in Acre erupt into open street fighting. Venetians and Genoese kill each other over warehouse rights and harbor access.
Drought in the Levant ruins crops across the coastal plain. The Crusader States depend increasingly on grain shipped from Sicily and Cyprus.
